--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.alpha_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Get alpha centrality for each node. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.alpha_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Get alpha centrality for each node. title: >- [Graph.alpha_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Get alpha centrality for each node. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get alpha centrality for each node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L63963-L64141){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.alpha_centrality( alpha=0.1, max_iter=100, tol=1e-06, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Alpha centrality](../assets/graphs/alpha-centrality.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same five-node directed graph shaded by alpha centrality with alpha 0.8, which follows outgoing edges. The source A, whose arcs reach every other node, scores 0.45, then B and C 0.17, D 0.13, and the sink E, which reaches nothing, only its exogenous share, 0.07." width="100%"} Alpha centrality is a generalization of eigenvector centrality that adds an exogenous factor: `x = α · A · x + e` where `α` is the attenuation factor, `A` is the adjacency matrix, and `e` is the exogenous factor (set to `1` for all nodes). Lower `α` emphasizes local neighborhood structure, while higher `α` considers more global structure. The returned scores are the fixed point of this equation, scaled to sum to `1`. The iteration converges only when `α` is below `1 / λ_max`, the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of `A`. Equivalently, a node's score counts the walks that *start* at it, with a walk of length `k` weighted by `α^k`. Every node gets a baseline of `1` from `e`, so, unlike plain eigenvector centrality, nodes outside strongly connected cores (including every node of an acyclic graph) still receive meaningful, non-zero scores. This makes alpha centrality a good choice for: - directed acyclic networks such as dependency, citation, or supply-chain graphs, where eigenvector centrality degenerates - measuring how much of the network a node can reach and influence through its outgoing edges - interpolating between degree-like (small `α`) and eigenvector-like (large `α`) rankings In a directed graph the sum runs over each node's successors, so the score reflects outgoing reach (see `katz_centrality()` for the incoming-edge counterpart). Edge weights are ignored. The fixed point is found by simple iteration starting from all-ones; if `α` is at or above `1 / λ_max` the values grow without bound; the method then emits a `RuntimeWarning` after `max_iter=` rounds (or as soon as the values overflow), and the returned scores are meaningless, so check `α` against the graph's spectrum when using large values. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [alpha]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.1]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Attenuation factor applied to each additional step of a walk. Defaults to `0.1`. Must be positive and below `1 / λ_max` for the iteration to converge (for an undirected graph `λ_max` is at least the average degree and at most the maximum degree; for a directed acyclic graph it is `0`, so any value works). Small values make the ranking close to (out-)degree; values approaching `1 / λ_max` make it approach eigenvector centrality. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of iterations. Defaults to `100`. If the scores have not converged by then, the values from the last iteration are normalized and returned without a warning. Convergence slows as `alpha=` approaches `1 / λ_max`, so increase this when using large `alpha=` values. [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-06]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Convergence threshold. Iteration stops once the largest relative change of any node's (unnormalized) score between two iterations falls below `tol=`. Defaults to `1e-6`. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name used to store the scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), the column is named `"alpha_centrality"`. An existing column with the same name is overwritten. Only used when `return_dict=` is `False`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the scores as a dictionary and leave the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), store the scores under `attr_name=` and return the graph for method chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to centrality scores, which sum to `1`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~katz_centrality`) : The same measure with a constant baseline. [](`~bonacich_power_centrality`) : Let ties to well-connected nodes count against a node. [](`~eigen_centrality`) : The limit with no outside status. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Alpha centrality follows outgoing edges, so in this small directed acyclic graph `A`, which reaches every other node, ranks first, and the sink `E`, which reaches nothing, keeps only its baseline share: ::: {#12bd14ae .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec dag = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")], directed=True, ) dag.alpha_centrality(alpha=0.8).get_node_df().select( "label", "alpha_centrality" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

It's the mirror image of `katz_centrality()`, which counts the chains leading in: ::: {#2fc95adc .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl citations = ( ec.citations() .alpha_centrality(alpha=0.5) .katz_centrality(alpha=0.5) ) cites = pl.col("label").map_elements( citations.get_out_degree, return_dtype=pl.Int64 ) ( citations.get_node_df() .with_columns(cites=cites) .select("label", "cites", "alpha_centrality", "katz_centrality") .sort("alpha_centrality", descending=True) .head(5) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

Drawn as a timeline, with the years running left to right, the scores rise toward the recent papers, while the two oldest papers, which cite nothing, have only their baseline: ::: {#667aa26e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} citations.plot( layout="pos", color_by="alpha_centrality", label_by="label" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: An `alpha=` close to `1 / lambda_max`, the reciprocal of the largest adjacency eigenvalue, makes the ranking approach `eigen_centrality()`; on an acyclic graph, any value converges. [Centrality](../user-guide/centrality.qmd#spectral-centrality) compares the spectral measures.
